e.etymology: A modern American name built on amor, Latin and Spanish for love, with the -i ending of Amari and Imani. Amori is also the Italian plural, loves.

e.meaning: Paecc's settlement (an Old English place name)
e.etymology: A respelling of Paxton, an English surname from villages named for an early settler called Paecc plus Old English tun, settlement. Pax, Latin for peace, is a popular but unrelated reading.
From Irish Brighid, Old Irish Brigit, from a Celtic word meaning high or exalted. It is the name of a pre-Christian Irish goddess and of Saint Brigid of Kildare; Bridget is the later English form.
namesakes: Saint Brigid of Kildare (5th-century abbess, a patron saint of Ireland)
Brigid O'Shaughnessy (femme fatale of The Maltese Falcon)

assoc.t: Celtic goddess of poetry, healing and smithcraft

e.etymology: An American elaboration of Mark with the -ell ending of Terrell and Darnell; Markell is also a surname. Mark comes from Latin Marcus, a name linked to the god Mars.
In American use a spelling of Aleah or Aliyah. Alea is also the Latin word for dice, as in Caesar's alea iacta est, the die is cast.
Made known by the R&B singer Jaheim, whose debut album came out in 2001. It follows the sound of Arabic names such as Raheem and Hakeem, with a Ja- opening.

assoc.t: Jaheim, R&B singer of the early 2000s

e.etymology: The Polish, Czech and Slovak form of Mark, from Latin Marcus with the Slavic -ek ending. Marcus is thought to derive from Mars, the Roman god of war.
From Arabic mahmud, praised or praiseworthy, the passive participle of hamida, to praise. It shares its root with Muhammad and Ahmad.
namesakes: Mahmoud Abbas (president of the Palestinian Authority)

e.etymology: A modern American name that reads as Cam, as in Cameron, plus Bree. It is close in sound to Cambria, the Latin name for Wales.
From Hebrew Nachum, consolation or comforter. Nahum is one of the twelve minor prophets of the Old Testament, whose short book foretells the fall of Nineveh.

assoc.t: Book of Nahum in the Old Testament

e.etymology: A surname meaning son of Morris or Maurice, a name from Latin Mauritius, Moorish. It is chiefly a Scottish surname.
namesakes: Jim Morrison (lead singer of the Doors)

assoc.t: Jim Morrison of the Doors and novelist Toni Morrison

e.etymology: A name used in India and by American families, close to Saniya, Arabic for exalted or radiant, and to Sanaa. Its own origin is not settled.
A respelling of Giovanni, the Italian form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
A variant of Finnegan, an Irish surname from Ó Fionnagáin, descendant of Fionnagán, a pet form of Fionn, fair or white.
A K spelling of Scarlett, an English surname for a dealer in scarlet cloth, from Old French escarlate. Scarlett O'Hara of Gone with the Wind turned the surname into a first name.
A spelling of Raelynn, a modern American blend of Rae and Lynn.
A respelling of Brinley, an English surname from a place name generally explained as Old English for a burnt clearing. The -leigh ending is a 2010s American fashion.
From Latin astra, stars, the plural of astrum, which comes from Greek astron. It is familiar from the motto ad astra, to the stars.

assoc.t: Latin phrase ad astra, to the stars
Astra, playable agent in the game Valorant

e.etymology: A respelling of Kailani, from Hawaiian kai, sea, and lani, sky or heaven, shaped here by the name Kayla.
A recent American coinage whose source is unclear; it shares its ending with Imani and Amani.
A form of Jamal, from Arabic jamal, beauty. Jamel is the usual spelling in French-speaking North Africa and a long-standing African American variant.
A spelling of Carly, a pet form of Carla and Caroline, the feminine forms of Carl and Charles, from Germanic karl, free man.
namesakes: Carli Lloyd (US soccer star, two-time Women's World Cup champion)

assoc.t: Carli Lloyd, US World Cup soccer champion

e.etymology: An African American coinage of the 1980s and 1990s, extending Deon in the pattern of Dante and Devonte.
The Spanish form of Greek Zenais, of Zeus, an early saint's name. Zenaida, the genus of the mourning dove, was named for Princess Zénaïde Bonaparte.

assoc.t: Zenaida, the genus of the mourning dove

e.etymology: A spelling of Kane, an Irish surname from Gaelic Ó Catháin, descendant of Cathán, a name based on cath, battle.
e.note: Often misread as Kanye; sounds the same as Kane and the Biblical Cain.

e.etymology: From Arabic hashim, one who breaks or crushes, a byname of the Prophet Muhammad's great-grandfather, remembered for breaking bread to feed pilgrims. The Hashemite dynasty of Jordan is named for him.
A Yiddish boys' name, the pet form of Lipman, from German Liebmann, dear man, often paired with the Hebrew name Yom Tov. In the US it is used mostly in Hasidic communities.

assoc.t: pop singer Dua Lipa, by surname

e.etymology: An African American name that took off in the 1960s and 1970s, possibly developed from Keziah, the Biblical daughter of Job, whose Hebrew name means cassia, a fragrant spice bark.
namesakes: Keisha Lance Bottoms (mayor of Atlanta, 2018 to 2022)

e.etymology: The German and Russian spelling of Isaac, from Hebrew Yitzhak, he laughs. In Genesis, Isaac is the son born to Abraham and Sarah in old age, named for Sarah's laughter at the news.
namesakes: Chris Isaak (singer of Wicked Game, by surname)

e.etymology: A spelling of Cody, an Irish surname from Gaelic Ó Cuidighthigh, descendant of the helpful one. Buffalo Bill Cody made the surname famous in the United States.
A variant of Aislinn, from Irish aisling, dream or vision, also the name of a genre of Irish poetry. In Ireland the name is said ASH-ling; the AYZ-lin pronunciation is American.
A pet form of Avis, Ava and Avery. It had a first run in the 1880s and has come back alongside Ava and Evie.
